record.paper_title: New results and open problems on subgraph centrality
record.original_question: Determine whether the examples in Figures 1 and 2 are truly minimal. More precisely, prove or disprove that the smallest graph with at least two interlacing values for exponential subgraph centrality has 9 vertices, and that the smallest graph with at least two interlacing values for resolvent centrality has 10 vertices.

evidence.quote: Figure 1: Graph with n = 9 nodes. It is the smallest graph we have found with at least two interlacing points: for vertices 2 and 8, the interlacing values are approximately β ≈ 2.12, 4.48.
Proving the minimality of these examples remains an open question.
Figure 2: Graph with n = 10 nodes. It is the smallest graph we have found with at least two interlacing values for resolvent centrality.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $G=(V,E)$ be a simple, undirected, connected graph on $n$ vertices with adjacency matrix $A$. For a parameter $\beta>0$, define the exponential subgraph centrality of vertex $i$ as
$$ SC_{\exp}(i;\beta) = [e^{\beta A}]_{ii}, $$
and, for $0<\alpha<1/\rho(A)$ (where $\rho(A)$ is the spectral radius of $A$), the resolvent subgraph centrality of vertex $i$ as
$$ SC_{\mathrm{res}}(i;\alpha) = [(I-\alpha A)^{-1}]_{ii}. $$
For two distinct vertices $i,j$, call a positive value of the parameter an interlacing value if the centralities of $i$ and $j$ are equal at that parameter while their ordering reverses on either side of it; equivalently, the function $\beta\mapsto SC_{\exp}(i;\beta)-SC_{\exp}(j;\beta)$ (respectively $\alpha\mapsto SC_{\mathrm{res}}(i;\alpha)-SC_{\mathrm{res}}(j;\alpha)$) vanishes and changes sign at that value. Say that $G$ has at least two interlacing values for exponential (respectively resolvent) subgraph centrality if there exists a pair of vertices for which the corresponding difference function has at least two positive sign-changing zeros.

Prove or disprove:
(a) The smallest connected graph that has at least two interlacing values for exponential subgraph centrality has exactly $9$ vertices.
(b) The smallest connected graph that has at least two interlacing values for resolvent subgraph centrality has exactly $10$ vertices.
artifact.status_search_result: The problem is posed as an explicit open question about the minimality of the smallest known examples (graphs on 9 and 10 vertices) exhibiting multiple interlacing values for exponential and resolvent subgraph centrality. A web search did not surface any subsequent work confirming or refuting these minimality claims; the problem appears to remain open.

status_evidence.title: New results and open problems on subgraph centrality
status_evidence.snippet: Listed as an open problem; proving minimality of the displayed small examples is stated as open.
status_evidence.claim: The minimality of the smallest known examples is left as an open question.

status_evidence.title: Matching exponential-based and resolvent-based centrality measures
status_evidence.snippet: Discusses comparisons between exponential and resolvent centralities but does not address minimal interlacing examples.
status_evidence.claim: Related work on these centralities does not resolve the minimality question.
